claim: The motor system combines different representations of object dynamics based on their reliability.
source: In a series of experiments, we show that the motor system combines different representations based on their reliability.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from four experiments showing weighted combinations of coordinate systems

claim: Noise creates an error between planned and executed force production which depends on the arm state.
source: Specifically, since noise creates an error between planned and executed force production which depends on the arm state, the motor system will rely more on the representation for which the plan is less affected.
evidence: Based on theoretical framework and computational modeling of noise effects

claim: The Re-Dyn mechanism can predict different results about dynamics representation and explain discrepancies between past studies.
source: In addition, we show that the same mechanism predicts the different results made about dynamics representation and thus explains the discrepancies between influential past studies.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulations of previous experimental designs

claim: There are at least three different reference frames that can solve the problem of representing dynamic mapping during object manipulation.
source: While this seems trivial, it is still unknown how we represent the dynamic mapping of such tasks, as there are at least three different reference frames that can solve this problem (Figure 1A).
evidence: Based on established motor control theory and illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: Forces can be represented as vectors in a Cartesian coordinate system located externally to the body.
source: First, we could use a Cartesian coordinate frame in which the forces are represented as vectors in a coordinate system located externally to the body.
evidence: Based on established motor control frameworks

claim: Forces can be represented using shoulder, elbow, and wrist joint torques.
source: Second, we could represent the forces using the shoulder, elbow, and wrist joint torques (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Forces can be represented as belonging to the hand or a hand-held object using the orientation vector connecting the shoulder and the object or hand in space.
source: Third, we could represent the forces as belonging to the hand or a hand-held object using the orientation vector connecting the shoulder and the object or hand in space (Berniker et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Previous studies have not provided a consistent view of dynamics representation in the motor system.
source: Although many studies have used dynamic generalization to address the topic of representation, the results do not provide a consistent view of the coordinate frame used by the motor system.
evidence: Based on review of multiple cited studies with conflicting conclusions

claim: Some studies support a Cartesian-based representation of dynamics.
source: Some studies support a Cartesian-based representation (Criscimagna-Hemminger et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Some studies support a joint-based representation of dynamics.
source: while others support a joint-based (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Some studies support an object-based representation of dynamics.
source: or object-based representation (Ahmed et al., 2008; Yeo et al., 2015; Franklin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Some studies suggest the motor system uses a mixture of coordinate frames.
source: In addition, some studies suggested that the system uses a mixture of the aforementioned coordinate frames (Parmar et al., 2011; Berniker et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: The motor system assigns different weights to each coordinate system solution and calculates a weighted sum.
source: We hypothesize that this inconsistency in results can be explained using a framework in which the motor system assigns different weights to each solution and calculates a weighted sum of these solutions.
evidence: Hypothesis tested through experimental data and modeling

claim: The Re-Dyn mechanism determines weights based on reliability rather than fitting them to data.
source: While we treat the problem similarly, we propose the Reliable Dynamics Representation (Re-Dyn) mechanism that determines the weights instead of fitting them.
evidence: Methodological approach described and tested experimentally

claim: The motor system prefers representations where force execution is more robust to distortion from neural noise.
source: According to our framework, the weights are calculated by considering the reliability of each representation during dynamic generalization. That is, the motor system prefers certain representations if the execution of forces based on this representation is more robust to distortion arising from neural noise.
evidence: Based on theoretical framework and computational modeling

claim: Participants adapted to the scaled curl force field as indicated by reduction in maximum perpendicular error.
source: Participants adapted to the force field as indicated by both the reduction in maximum perpendicular error, measuring how much the force field perturbed the participants from moving in a straight line towards the target (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Participants adapted to the scaled curl force field as indicated by increase in predictive force compensation profile.
source: and the increase in predictive force compensation profile in the training workspace (Figure 3C, gray curve) that resembles the cosine tuning of the scaled force field (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3C and 2D

claim: In experiment 1, the force compensation profile in the training workspace did not shift with respect to the force field curve.
source: For the curve calculated based on movements in the training workspace (Figure 3C, gray curve) we did not find a shift with respect to the curve of the force field (–0.01±0.03°, mean±STD).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: In experiment 1, test workspace 1 showed a leftward shift of –23.0±4.8° in the force compensation curve.
source: For the predictive force compensation curve in test workspace 1 (Figure 3C, blue curve), we found a leftward shift of –23.0±4.8° with respect to the force field curve.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: In experiment 1, test workspace 2 showed a leftward shift of –6.3±4.8° in the force compensation curve.
source: For the predictive force compensation curve in test workspace 2 (Figure 3C, red curve) we again found a leftward shift of the curve, however, this shift (–6.3±4.8°) was smaller compared with the shift we found for test workspace 1.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: A decrease in generalized force magnitude may be due to the distance between training and test workspaces.
source: Based on previous studies such a decrease in generalized force magnitude might be due to the distance between the training and test workspaces (Gandolfo et al., 1996; Berniker et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on citations to previous work

claim: None of the individual coordinate reference frames could predict the shifts in force compensation in experiment 1 test workspaces.
source: Importantly, none of the individual coordinate systems can accurately capture the experimental force compensation trend of the participants.
evidence: Demonstrated through comparison of model predictions with experimental data

claim: The Re-Dyn model accurately predicted the force compensation trend in experiment 1 test workspace 1.
source: However, when combining the three coordinate systems according to Re-Dyn-based weights (Figure 3E, upper panel), we could accurately predict this force compensation trend (Figure 3E, bottom panel).
evidence: Demonstrated through comparison of model predictions with experimental data

claim: The Re-Dyn prediction uses no information from experimental results except amplitude scaling.
source: Despite the fact that the Re-Dyn prediction uses no information from the experimental results with the exception of the amplitude scaling, the prediction almost perfectly fits the complex pattern of forces produced by the experimental participants.
evidence: Methodological description of the modeling approach

claim: In experiment 2, the training workspace predictive force compensation curve was not shifted with respect to the force field.
source: Similar to experiment 1, the predictive force compensation curve in the training workspace was not shifted with respect to the curve of the force field (–1±2.45°, mean ±STD).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: In experiment 2, test workspace 1 showed a rightward shift of 34.5±1.2° in the force compensation curve.
source: For the predictive force compensation curve in test workspace 1 (Figure 4C, blue curve), we found a rightward shift of 34.5±1.2° with respect to the actual force field.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: In experiment 2, test workspace 2 showed a rightward shift of 15.4±4.4° in the force compensation curve.
source: For the predictive force compensation curve in test workspace 2 (Figure 4C, red curve) we again found a significant rightward shift, however, this shift of 15.4±4.4° was smaller than that of test workspace 1.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: A different pattern of weights was found in experiment 2 compared with experiment 1, representing changes in noise sensitivity due to different arm configurations.
source: Importantly, we found a different pattern of weights in experiment 2 compared with experiment 1 which represents the changes in noise sensitivity due to the different arm configurations.
evidence: Based on comparison of model predictions across experiments

claim: In experiment 3, the arm posture did not change between adaptation and generalization parts.
source: That is, the arm posture did not change between the adaptation and generalization parts of the experiment.
evidence: Experimental design description

claim: In experiment 3, the training workspace force compensation curve did not shift with respect to the force field.
source: For the predictive force compensation curve in the training workspace (Figure 5C, gray curve) we did not find a shift with respect to the force field (–0.05±0.14°, mean±STD).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: In experiment 3, test workspace 1 showed a rightward shift of 17±5.7° in the force compensation curve despite no changes in arm posture.
source: However, for the force compensation curve in test workspace 1, we found a rightward shift of 17±5.7° (Figure 5C, blue curve) despite no changes in the arm posture.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: In experiment 3, test workspace 2 showed a rightward shift of 4.5±3.6° in the force compensation curve.
source: In test workspace 2 we again found a rightward shift of the predictive force compensation curve, however, this shift (4.5±3.6°) was smaller compared with the shift we found for test workspace 1 (Figure 5C, red curve).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: In experiment 3, both Cartesian and joint-based representations predict no shift in force compensation curve for test workspaces.
source: In this experiment, since the arm configuration did not change between the training and test workspaces, both the Cartesian and joint-based representations predict that the force compensation curve for the test workspaces will not shift compared with the force compensation curve for the training workspace.
evidence: Based on theoretical predictions from coordinate system models

claim: In experiment 4, the training workspace predictive force compensation curve did not significantly shift with respect to the force field.
source: Again, the training workspace predictive force compensation curve (Figure 6C, gray curve) did not significantly shift with respect to the original force field curve (–0.03±0.07°, mean±STD).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: In experiment 4, test workspace 1 showed a small leftward shift of –3.7±3.1° in the force compensation curve.
source: For test workspace 1, we found a small leftward shift of –3.7±3.1° (Figure 6C, blue curve)
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: In experiment 4, test workspace 2 showed a rightward shift of 6.8±1.8° in the force compensation curve.
source: and for test workspace 2 we found a rightward shift of 6.8±1.8° (Figure 6C, red curve).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: In experiment 4, the Cartesian and object-based representations are the more dominant reference frames.
source: We found that in general, the Cartesian and object-based representations are the more dominant reference frames as evidenced by the predicted weights (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: Based on Re-Dyn model predictions

claim: The Re-Dyn model has less prediction error compared to energy-based and smoothness-based models.
source: Across the eight generalization test workspaces we had in the four experiments, we found that the Re-Dyn model has less prediction error, as measured by the error between the prediction and experimental force compensation curves (Figure 7C)
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions across all experiments

claim: The Re-Dyn model better predicts the phase shift of the force compensation curve compared to alternative models.
source: and better predicts the phase shift of the force compensation curve (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions across all experiments

claim: The Re-Dyn model was superior to other models when accounting for additional degrees of freedom using BIC.
source: We observed that the Re-Dyn was superior to the other models, including the fitted optimal model, when accounting for the additional degrees of freedom (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by BIC analysis of model comparisons

claim: The Re-Dyn model can explain the results of Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994.
source: We found that the simulation results, specifically the direction of deviation from the straight-line path, can capture the experimental results (Figure 8E).
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation of previous experimental design

claim: In the Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi 1994 study, the joint and object-based coordinate systems predict similar patterns of generalized forces.
source: Simulating this experimental protocol, we found that the force pattern of the joint and object-based coordinate system is similar (Figure 8B)
evidence: Based on simulation of previous experimental design

claim: Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi 1994 could not differentiate between joint and object coordinate systems based on their experimental design.
source: Since the authors did not consider the object-based coordinate system, they concluded that the observed generalization is a result of the motor system using the joint-based coordinate system, although it is impossible to differentiate between the joint or object coordinate systems based on this design.
evidence: Based on analysis of previous study's methodology and results

claim: The motor system uses a mix of force representation with greater weight to the representation that is less variable in extrapolated force production.
source: Our idea suggests that the motor system uses a mix of force representation with a greater weight to the representation that is less variable in extrapolated force production.
evidence: Summary of the main theoretical framework

claim: The motor system alternates between controlled variables to reduce the effect of noise aside from optimizing the trajectory.
source: While the idea of trajectory planning while minimizing the effect of noise was presented by Harris and Wolpert, 1998, we show that the motor system alternates between controlled variables, that is, end-point, joints, or object-based forces, in order to reduce the effect of noise aside from optimizing the trajectory.
evidence: Based on experimental results and comparison with previous work

claim: Signal-dependent noise could change the weighting between coordinate systems as a function of movement direction.
source: For signal-dependent noise, the noise characteristics change as a function of the forces the muscles need to produce. In this case, since different reference frames predict different levels of force for different movement directions, elevated noise can increase the planned forces corruption of one reference frame compared to others, changing the weighting between coordinate systems.
evidence: Theoretical speculation about alternative noise models

claim: The cerebellum has been proposed to host both forward and inverse internal models.
source: The cerebellum has been proposed to host both types of internal models (Wolpert and Kawato, 1998; Smith and Shadmehr, 2005)
evidence: Based on citations to previous work

claim: Changes in premotor cortex activity were evident during force field adaptation.
source: For example, changes in premotor cortex (PMd) activity were also evident during force field adaptation (Perich et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on citation to previous work

claim: Force representation relies on all three coordinate systems with specific weights that change between generalization scenarios.
source: Other combinations that include a single or two coordinate system can explain some of the results but not all of them, suggesting that force representation relies on all three with specific weights that change between generalization scenarios.
evidence: Based on comparison of different model combinations across experiments

claim: Thirty-two right-handed participants participated in the study, with eight participants per experiment.
source: Thirty-two right-handed participants (14 females; aged between 22–35) participated in one of four experiments (eight participants per experiment)
evidence: Methodological description of participant recruitment

claim: The experimental protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Medical Faculty of the Technical University of Munich.
source: The experimental protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Medical Faculty of the Technical University of Munich (number 763/20 S-KH).
evidence: Statement of ethical approval

claim: The vBOT robotic device recorded hand position and velocity while generating force feedback at 1 kHz in real-time.
source: The robotic device was used to record hand position and velocity while generating force feedback at 1 kHz in real-time.
evidence: Methodological description of experimental apparatus

claim: A six-axis force transducer measured end-point forces applied by the participant on the handle at 1 kHz.
source: A six-axis force transducer (ATI Nano 25; ATI Industrial Automation) measured the end-point forces applied by the participant on the handle and was also sampled at 1 kHz.
evidence: Methodological description of experimental apparatus

claim: Participants' arms were supported on an air sled allowing frictionless movement.
source: The participant grasped the robotic handle using his/her right hand with their arm supported on an air sled allowing frictionless movement.
evidence: Methodological description of experimental setup

claim: Participants did not fix their wrist joints during the experiment, similar to previous studies.
source: During the experiment, we assume participants maintain a fixed wrist angle and thus we did not fix their wrist joints similar to previous studies (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994; Shadmehr and Moussavi, 2000; Malfait et al., 2002; Malfait et al., 2005).
evidence: Methodological description with citations to previous work

claim: Wrist deviation during force field and generalization experiments was shown to be small and have negligible effect.
source: The wrist deviation during force field and generalization experiments was shown to be small and thus have a negligible effect (Berniker et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on citation to previous work

claim: The start and target points were chosen from 16 equally spaced locations on a 10 cm diameter circle.
source: The start and target points were chosen from 16 equally spaced locations on a 10 cm diameter circle (Figure 2B).
evidence: Methodological description of experimental design

claim: Participants were instructed to move with a consistent peak speed of 50 cm/s.
source: Participants were instructed to move with a consistent peak speed of 50 cm/s.
evidence: Methodological description of experimental instructions

claim: Peak speed within ±8 cm/s from the desired peak speed was considered 'good'.
source: Peak speed that was within ±8 cm/s from the desired peak speed was considered 'good' while a peak speed below this value received a 'too slow' message and above it received a 'too fast' message.
evidence: Methodological description of performance feedback criteria

claim: The force channel was created by generating forces perpendicular to the line connecting start and target positions.
source: The virtual walls were created by generating forces that were perpendicular to the line connecting the start and target positions.
evidence: Methodological description of force channel implementation

claim: The force channel stiffness coefficient was 4000 N/m and damping coefficient was 2 Ns/m.
source: The forces were calculated according to the deviation of the hand position from the straight-line path multiplied by a stiffness coefficient of 4000 N/m and the velocity in the movement perpendicular direction multiplied by a damping coefficient of 2 Ns/m.
evidence: Methodological description of force channel parameters

claim: The forces during force field trials were calculated using a scaled curl matrix.
source: The forces were calculated using a scaled curl matrix.
evidence: Methodological description of force field implementation

claim: In experiment 1, the training workspace center was set with shoulder joint at 50° and elbow joint at 90°.
source: The location of the center of the training workspace was set for each participant so that the participants' shoulder joint was at 50° and elbow joint was at 90°.
evidence: Methodological description of experiment 1 workspace configuration

claim: In experiment 1, test workspace 1 center was set with shoulder angle at 50° and elbow angle at 55°.
source: The center of test workspace 1 was set so with participants' shoulder angle at 50° and elbow angle at 55°.
evidence: Methodological description of experiment 1 workspace configuration

claim: In experiment 1, test workspace 2 center was set with shoulder joint at 75° and elbow at 45°.
source: The center of test workspace 2 was set with the shoulder joint at 75° and the elbow at 45° (Figure 3A).
evidence: Methodological description of experiment 1 workspace configuration

claim: In experiment 2, the training workspace center was set with shoulder joint at 40° and elbow joint at 70°.
source: The location of the center of the training workspace was set for each participant so that the participants' shoulder joint was at 40° and elbow joint was at 70°.
evidence: Methodological description of experiment 2 workspace configuration

claim: In experiment 2, test workspace 1 center was set with shoulder angle at 75° and elbow angle at 85°.
source: The center of test workspace 1 was set so with participants' shoulder angle at 75° and elbow angle at 85°.
evidence: Methodological description of experiment 2 workspace configuration

claim: In experiment 2, test workspace 2 center was set with shoulder joint at 75° and elbow at 50°.
source: The center of test workspace 2 was set with the shoulder joint at 75° and the elbow at 50° (Figure 4A).
evidence: Methodological description of experiment 2 workspace configuration

claim: In experiment 3, the participant's hand always moved in the training workspace.
source: However, in this experiment, the participant's hand always moved in the training workspace (both training and test workspaces).
evidence: Methodological description of experiment 3 design

claim: In experiment 3, movements in test workspaces were performed using a virtual pole attached to the participant's hand.
source: Movements in the test workspaces were performed using a virtual pole attached to the participants' hand.
evidence: Methodological description of experiment 3 design

claim: In experiment 4, the training workspace center was set with shoulder joint at 55° and elbow joint at 75°.
source: The center of the training workspace was set for each participant so that their shoulder joint was at 55° and elbow joint was at 75°.
evidence: Methodological description of experiment 4 workspace configuration

claim: In experiment 4, test workspace 1 and 2 centers were set at shoulder and elbow joints of [30°, 100°] and [80°, 50°], respectively.
source: The center of test workspaces 1 and 2 was set such that the shoulder and elbow joints were oriented at [30°, 100°] and [80°, 50°], respectively.
evidence: Methodological description of experiment 4 workspace configuration

claim: Experiment 4 workspace locations kept the hand orientation constant while the arm configuration varied.
source: These workspace locations kept the hand orientation constant while the arm configuration varied.
evidence: Methodological description of experiment 4 design rationale

claim: Maximum perpendicular error measures how much the force field perturbed participants from moving in a straight line towards the target.
source: On each null field or force field trial, the maximum distance between the trajectory and the straight line joining the start and target points was calculated as a measure of kinematic error.
evidence: Methodological description of data analysis measure

claim: Force compensation was calculated as the regression slope between the perfect force compensation signal and the recorded force signal.
source: Force compensation was calculated as the regression slope between the perfect force compensation signal, the independent variable, and the recorded force signal, the dependent variable (Smith et al., 2006).
evidence: Methodological description with citation to previous work

claim: For Cartesian representation, the forces are invariant with respect to arm orientation.
source: For this representation, the forces are invariant with respect to the arm orientation.
evidence: Theoretical property of Cartesian coordinate system

claim: For joint-based representation, the generalized forces should differ from learned forces when arm configuration changes.
source: For this representation, the generalized forces exhibited in the test workspaces should differ from the learned forces since the arm configuration has changed.
evidence: Theoretical property of joint-based coordinate system

claim: For object-based representation, the motor system relates the dynamics to a grasped object.
source: For this representation, the motor system relates the dynamics to a grasped object.
evidence: Theoretical property of object-based coordinate system

claim: For object-based representation, expected forces are calculated according to the orientation of the held object when moving outside the training workspace.
source: When moving outside of the training workspace, the expected forces are calculated according to the orientation of the held object, which is rotated with the hand orientation.
evidence: Theoretical property of object-based coordinate system

claim: The reliability of each reference frame was defined as how much it is affected by noise and diverts from a non-corrupted dynamic generalization pattern.
source: The reliability of each reference frame was defined as how much it is affected by noise and divert from a non-corrupted dynamic generalization pattern.
evidence: Methodological description of Re-Dyn model

claim: For the joint and object coordinate systems, additive noise values were drawn from a normal distribution with zero mean and variance equal to 1°.
source: For the joint and object coordinate systems the additive noise values were drawn from a normal distribution with zero mean and variance equal to 1°.
evidence: Methodological description of noise modeling parameters

claim: 1° variance in joint angles corresponds to ~1.7 mm variance in end-point coordinates for a movement radius of 10 cm.
source: This corresponds to ~1.7 mm variance in end-point coordinates (Cartesian coordinate system) for a movement radius of 10 cm.
evidence: Calculation based on arc length formula

claim: A decay factor was used to match the amplitude between predicted and experimental force compensation profiles.
source: Thus, in order to match the observed behavioral force compensation patterns and the predicted force compensation pattern, we multiplied the force compensation profile of the combined model in (Equation 6) with a decay factor that set an equal amplitude between the predicted and experimental force compensation profiles
evidence: Methodological description of model fitting procedure

claim: For the energy-based model, the motor system gives more weight to reference frames requiring less energy to produce generalized forces.
source: According to this criterion, for each movement direction the motor system will rely more on reference frames which require less energy to produce the pattern of generalized forces.
evidence: Methodological description of alternative model

claim: Energy was quantified as the force profile mean for each reference frame.
source: Since energy is proportional to the magnitude of required forces, we quantified the amount of energy needed by each reference frame as the force profile mean.
evidence: Methodological description of energy calculation

claim: For the smoothness-based model, the motor system relies more on reference frames where the force profile is smoother.
source: Based on this hypothesis, we tested whether the motor system relies more on reference frames in which the force profile is smoother.
evidence: Methodological description of alternative model

claim: Smoothness was calculated using the mean value of the third temporal derivative of the force profile.
source: For this purpose, we calculated the smoothness using the mean value of the third temporal derivative of the force profile predicted by each reference frame.
evidence: Methodological description of smoothness calculation

claim: The optimal weights were constrained to positive values with sum equal to or less than one.
source: For this optimization problem, we constrained the weights to positive values and set the sum of the weights to be equal to or less than one.
evidence: Methodological description of optimization constraints

claim: To predict weights for previous studies, the same simulations were repeated while changing workspace locations and force field type according to each study.
source: To find the predicted weights of the Re-Dyn model for previous studies, we repeated the same simulations similar to the simulations we performed based on the experimental design reported here while changing the training and test workspace locations and the type of force field according to each study.
evidence: Methodological description of retrospective analysis

claim: Workspace locations for previous studies were set based on joint angles for a two-link arm with upper arm length 33 cm and forearm length 34 cm.
source: Workspaces locations were set based on the joints angles (Figure 8) for a two-link arm with lengths 33 and 34 cm for the upper arm and forearm, respectively, that were used in Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994.
evidence: Methodological description of retrospective analysis parameters
